paragraphs: The one who makes the law knows better than anyone how it should be carried out and interpreted. It seems, then, that no constitution could be better than one in which the executive and legislative powers are united. Yet this very fact makes such a government inadequate in certain respects, because things that ought to be kept distinct are confused, and the prince and the Sovereign, being the same person, form, so to speak, nothing more than a government without a government.

It is not good for the one who makes the laws to execute them, or for the body of the people to turn its attention away from general concerns and give it to particular objects. Nothing is more dangerous than the influence of private interests in public affairs. The abuse of the laws by the government is a lesser evil than the corruption of the legislator, which inevitably follows from a particular point of view. In that case, since the State is altered in its very substance, all reform becomes impossible. A people that never misused the powers of government would never misuse its independence; a people that always governed well would have no need to be governed.

Taken strictly, the word democracy describes something that has never existed and never will. It goes against the natural order for the many to govern and the few to be governed. We cannot imagine the people staying permanently in session to handle public affairs, and plainly they cannot appoint commissions to do it for them without changing the form of the administration.

In fact, I can state confidently as a principle that when the functions of government are shared among several bodies, the smaller ones sooner or later gain the greatest authority, if only because they are in a position to dispatch business quickly, and power thus naturally falls into their hands.

Besides, how many conditions that are hard to bring together does such a government require! First, a very small State, where the people can easily be assembled and where each citizen can readily know all the others. Second, great simplicity of manners, to keep business from multiplying and raising thorny problems. Next, a large measure of equality in rank and fortune, without which equality of rights and authority cannot last long. Lastly, little or no luxury — for luxury either comes from riches or makes them necessary. It corrupts rich and poor alike: the rich through possession and the poor through covetousness. It sells the country to softness and vanity, and takes all its citizens away from the State, to make them slaves to one another, and all of them slaves to public opinion.

This is why a famous writer made virtue the fundamental principle of Republics, for all these conditions could not exist without virtue. But he did not make the necessary distinctions, and so that great thinker was often inexact and sometimes obscure. He did not see that, since sovereign authority is the same everywhere, the same principle should be found in every well-constituted State, to a greater or lesser degree, it is true, depending on the form of government.

I would add that no government is so liable to civil wars and internal upheaval as democratic or popular government. None tends so strongly and so constantly to turn into some other form, and none, as it stands, needs more vigilance and courage to keep going. Under such a constitution above all, the citizen should arm himself with strength and steadfastness, and repeat every day of his life what a virtuous Count Palatine[1] said in the Diet of Poland: Malo periculosam libertatem quam quietum servitium.
A people of gods would govern itself democratically. A government so perfect does not suit men.
Lorraine. I prefer liberty with danger to peace with slavery.
